newsitem.title: USA: DEA confirms death of Mexican drug lord.
newsitem.headline: DEA confirms death of Mexican drug lord.

text.p: The U.S. anti-drug agency on Sunday confirmed the death of one of Mexico's most notorious drug kingpins and said it would significantly disrupt Mexican drug-trafficking operations.

Amado Carrillo Fuentes, nicknamed "Lord of the Skies" for his use of commercial airplanes to fly tons of cocaine from Colombia to Mexico, was reported to have died on Friday in Mexico City in a private clinic while undergoing plastic surgery.

"Amado Carrillo-Fuentes was arguably the most powerful drug trafficker in Mexico," Drug Enforcement Administrator Thomas Constantine said in a statement confirming Carrillo's death. "The disruption his death will cause among Mexican drug trafficking organisations will be significant."

Mexican authorities have not yet confirmed Carrillo's death, saying they needed more tests to confirm the identity of the man who died of a heart attack after extensive plastic surgery and liposuction.
The drug baron's organised crime group, based in Juarez, is associated with Colombia's Cali Cartel and has many regional bases in Northern Mexico.

Carrillo, believed to be 42, was the subject of more than 25 separate Mexican and U.S. law enforcement investigations. He had been indicted twice in Miami, in 1988 and again in 1996, as well as in Dallas in 1993.
At the time of his death, Carrillo was attempting to consolidate control over drug trafficking along the entire northern border of Mexico, Constantine said.
"Law enforcement on both sides of the border should capitalise on the ensuing confusion and we should redouble our efforts to destroy his organisation," Constantine said.
This is the second of the top Mexican drug barons to "pass from power," Barry McCaffrey, director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy, said in a statement.

"The continuing cooperation of the U.S. and Mexico is vital to keep up the relentless law enforcement pressure that forced Carrillo Fuentes to undergo appearance altering surgery that cost him his life," McCaffrey said.
The arrest, trial and imprisonment in the U.S. of Juan Garcia Abrego is considered the first major U.S.-Mexican law enforcement victory, McCaffrey said.
